solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Say a bit more than this?

definitions.text: Say a bit more than this?

parts.words: Say a bit more than this?
parts.note: to have your say is to offer an opinion; a modest opinion is worth a couple of pence, and saying a bit more would go beyond that small coin's worth

explanation.surface: A puzzled question to a speaker who seems to have stopped short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is a noun here, your say in a debate; 'a bit more' hints at a small coin, so a little more than this would exceed the value of a tiny opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: Offering one's modest opinion is giving one's two-penny contribution, an idiom for a small say in a discussion.

clue.text: Material that's droll, funny in a small way

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the shortened way

parts.note: way made small by dropping its A gives WY, also a standard abbreviation of way

indicators.note: funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters of droll are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something droll described as amusing in a modest manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' is an adjective meaning concerned with physical things, not cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A materialistic outlook, focused on earthly possessions rather than the spiritual, is a synonym of the adjective.

clue.text: Copper mine — coal's replaced copper

parts.note: a copper coin is a penny, abbreviated P

indicators.note: replaced means put back in a different place, so the letters of mine and coal are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mining note: a pit once dug for coal now yields copper instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'copper mine' as a mine for the metal; the first 'Copper' is the slang for an officer and the second is a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is long-standing British slang for an officer of the law.

clue.text: Students gathering for one hot tipple

indicators.note: gathering means collecting in, so the students' union surrounds the example

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students in the UK
for one means for example, abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: A group of students getting together for a hot drink each.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional warm drink of wine, hot water, sugar and spice, named after an eighteenth-century colonel.

clue.text: Row about carbon part of a wind instrument

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the oar goes round the carbon

parts.note: to row is to pull an oar
C is the chemical symbol for carbon
to be in something is to be part of it

explanation.surface: An argument over carbon in some component of a woodwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel but is the rowing stroke; 'part of' looks like it points to a component.
explanation.definitionFit: A small egg-shaped flute of clay with finger holes, played by blowing, is a classic wind instrument.

clue.text: Wood's height through pass

indicators.note: through means running inside, so height sits within the pass

parts.note: a pass for entry is a ticket

explanation.surface: A forest's elevation viewed through a mountain gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pass' looks like a mountain pass but is a permit; 's is a link meaning 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense clump of trees and shrubs is a small wood.

clue.text: Mr Morton wants a jacket, full of a head cold

indicators.note: full of means containing, so the jacket holds the other letters

parts.note: a bomber is a short zipped jacket
a head means apiece, the same as each
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: A man called Morton needs a coat because his head is stuffy with a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: J.B. Morton wrote the long-running Daily Express humour column 'By the Way' under a pen name meaning a scavenger of the shoreline.
explanation.definitionFit: J.B. Morton was a British humorist who used this pen name for his newspaper column for half a century.

clue.text: Part of flower has little weight, I agree!

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for a stone, a British unit of weight
amen is said to express agreement

explanation.surface: Someone agreeing that a bit of a bloom weighs very little.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds; 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The pollen-producing male organ of a bloom, made of a filament and anther.

clue.text: Goes off into stand around racing circuit

indicators.note: around means turned round, so the whole combination is read backwards
into puts the decaying word inside the stand

parts.note: to stand or stay in place is to lie, as a ball lies where it stopped
food that goes off rots

explanation.surface: Something spoiling inside a grandstand at a motor-racing track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stand' here means stay put, as a ball lies where it stopped; 'around' turns the whole assembled LIROTSE back to front, not just the stand.
explanation.definitionFit: The Portuguese town near Lisbon has a motor-racing track that once hosted the Grand Prix.

clue.text: Soldiers will guard shop for nothing

indicators.note: guard means surround protectively, so the soldiers enclose the informer

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers
to shop someone is British slang for informing on them, to rat

explanation.surface: Troops protecting a store without charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shop' is the verb meaning to betray to the police, not a store.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin-derived word for free of charge, given without payment.

clue.text: Caught her up, put on manacles

indicators.note: manacles means holds fast, so the added word encloses the reversed pronoun

parts.note: something put on at the end is appended

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word her is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A woman arrested and put in handcuffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manacles' is a verb here: APPENDED holds REH, her reversed by 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrested or seized by police, the usual sense of taking someone into custody.

clue.text: Funny business consultant?

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business
a hospital consultant is a senior doctor, a medic

explanation.surface: Asking whether a firm's adviser is amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consultant' looks like a business adviser but is a hospital specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to comedy, so humorous or amusing.

clue.text: Credit for cutting down criminal activity

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the credit goes inside the drink

parts.note: to down a drink is to sup it
on tick is British slang for on credit

explanation.surface: Using credit to reduce crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting down' looks like reducing; 'down' is the drinking verb and 'cutting' the insertion signal. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An armed robbery, where victims are held at gunpoint, is a crime.

clue.text: Bear not against finding rabbit

indicators.note: not means without, so the letter for against is dropped

parts.note: to bear something is to carry or convey it
V, short for versus, means against

explanation.surface: A bear that is not opposed to discovering a bunny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' is the verb meaning carry, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a rabbit, also its fur.

clue.text: Irrational character got stuff initially confused

indicators.note: the first letters of the two words are confused, swapped between them

parts.note: got means had
stuff means substance, matter

explanation.surface: Someone muddled from the outset about what they had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially confused' swaps the initial letters of HAD and MATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: The crazed hatmaker of the tea party in Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland is a famous irrational figure.

clue.text: One name rejected by Disneyland, disastrously wrong

indicators.note: disastrously means in ruinous disorder, so the remaining letters are rearranged
rejected by means thrown out of, so a single N leaves the theme park's letters

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name, taken once

explanation.surface: One person turned away by the theme park, which went badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Disneyland has two Ns; only one is dropped, and the remaining DISEYLAND is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Pride, greed and the rest of the seven cardinal vices are each a grave moral wrong.

clue.text: I moan about eating perfectly served fruit salad

indicators.note: eating means taking inside, so the shuffled letters surround the serve
about means around in disorder, so the letters of I moan are rearranged

parts.note: in tennis, a perfect unreturnable serve is an ace, so served perfectly is aced

explanation.surface: Someone complaining while a fruit dessert is being eaten after being dished up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges I MOAN into MONIA, which 'eating' wraps round ACED.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish of mixed diced fruit or vegetables, named after the ethnically mixed region of the Balkans.

clue.text: Remedy to get round bereavement, mostly?

definitions.text: Remedy to get round bereavement, mostly?

indicators.note: get round means surround, so the remedy encloses the shortened loss

parts.note: a remedy is a cure

indicators.note: mostly means most of it, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a bereavement is a loss

explanation.surface: Asking whether the cure for grief is mostly a way of coping.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a sense of resolution is what heals most grief.
explanation.definitionFit: A feeling of finality and emotional resolution after a death helps the bereaved move on.

clue.text: Tackle blunder admitted by detective

indicators.note: admitted by means let inside, so the mistake goes within the detective

parts.note: dick is slang for a private detective
to blunder is to err

explanation.surface: An investigator confessing to a mistake in handling something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tackle' is lifting gear, not a challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: Tackle means hoisting apparatus, and a crane for lifting heavy loads is such gear.

clue.text: A level playing field

definitions.meaning: a level on a scale, as in the height of a note or degree of intensity
a sports field, as for football or cricket

explanation.surface: A fair contest where no side has an advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'level playing field' hides the split: 'A level' and 'playing field'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a degree or level of intensity and a ground on which sport is played.

clue.text: River, pool, and old coat

parts.note: a pot is a pool of money staked in a game
a mac is a raincoat, short for mackintosh

explanation.surface: A list of things by the water: a river, a pond, and a worn coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pool' is a kitty of money, not water.
explanation.definitionFit: The waterway flowing through Washington DC is a major American river.

clue.text: Blow rings — exquisite!

parts.note: to blow a horn is to toot
rings are shaped like the letter O, so two rings give OO

explanation.surface: A command to blow smoke rings, admired as superb.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is an old affected term of praise for something excessively refined.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned affected term for something extremely or excessively refined or precious.

clue.text: Peugeot tyre is regularly given pressure for self-inflation

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the words is taken

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for pressure in physics

explanation.surface: A French car's tyre gets pumped up on its own.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface of tyre pressure and inflation hides a vanity jaunt.
explanation.definitionFit: An indulgent act undertaken to boost one's own vanity puffs up the self.

clue.text: Opening up an atheist

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the gap is read from bottom to top

parts.note: an opening is a gap

explanation.surface: An atheist starting to talk openly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening up' suggests confiding; 'up' reverses the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen, one outside the main religions, is loosely an unbeliever.

clue.text: Persuaded to keep time — personal setback

indicators.note: keep means hold, so the led contains the time

parts.note: to persuade someone is to lead them, so persuaded is led
own means personal, belonging to oneself

explanation.surface: Talked into keeping to schedule, and then a private disappointment.
explanation.definitionFit: A disappointment or anticlimax is a setback.

clue.text: In castle one will be buried in manure

indicators.note: buried in means placed inside, so the castle and one go into the manure

parts.note: manure is dung
in chess the castle is the rook, abbreviated R
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Inside a castle, someone will end up buried in muck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' at the start is the definition, in the sense 'in the course of', not part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: In and the answer both mean throughout or in the course of a period, as in 'in the night'.

clue.text: The speaker interrupts rather short celebrity

indicators.note: interrupts means breaks into, so me goes into the shortened word
short means cut off at the end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: I would rather means I would sooner
a speaker refers to themselves as me

explanation.surface: A speaker cutting in on a not-very-famous person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rather short' reads as 'fairly short' but is SOONER cut short to SOONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of some importance or fame, as in 'she thinks she's a real somebody'.

clue.text: Keep kissing, even

definitions.meaning: to neck is to kiss, so necking and then necking again is to keep kissing
even means level, with neither side ahead in a race

explanation.surface: Advice to a couple: carry on smooching, it's all square.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is cryptic: the verb 'neck' (kiss) joined to itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes competitors level with each other, so the race is even.
